utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today we'll first start with the examination of the next Defence witness, and Ms. Radovanovic will join us later today. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which I understand is Mr. Segers?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I also understand that there's translation in the Dutch language. I might not need that much of it, but, nevertheless, welcome. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And we find ... I see we're on channel 7 for Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Segers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Do you understand -- do you receive translation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was whether you received translation into your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do hear you weak. Not loud enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In what language do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. And, Mr. Usher -- and in what language do you hear me or do you receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear the interpretation, but I also hear the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that in your earphones, you receive interpretation, whereas directly you can hear me although in the English language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Segers. Mr. Segers, I'm speaking English to you because English and French are the official languages of this Tribunal, although I will follow your testimony in the language you speak yourself. Mr. Segers, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: My name is Jan Segers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have a look at 1D05961 in e-court, and I have a hard copy for the witness in his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Shortly, sir, you will see on the screen and receive a document.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask that you look at the original language version, and my question would be: Do you remember giving this statement to the Belgian authorities on the date that is indicated?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the last page of the document in both languages, and there's a signature on this last page. Whose signature is on the statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we now have Dutch on the left part of our screens. I looked into e-court. I see two versions. Is it true that we only have the Dutch and the English version and that there's no B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. CLSS does not translate things into B/C/S for the Defence until after they are used in court as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, if Mr. Mladic has any problems with specific portions, then of course he should be assisted in understanding and to be able to fully follow the examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you voluntarily give this statement to the Belgian authorities on the date indicated?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that I voluntarily made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by everything in the statement as correctly written or do you wish to correct anything?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: No, I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If asked today the same questions as in the statement, would your answers today in court be, in essence, the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: The questions would be the same -- excuse me, the statement would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Having taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just check. I heard you say [Dutch spoken], but I take it that you wanted to refer to the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, having taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth today, does that mean that we can consider your answers in the written statement to be truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I can only confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could take a look at 1D05960, of which I also have an original in a language that the witness also understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Shortly, sir, another document will appear on your screen and will be available to you in hard copy and then I'll have some questions. On the left of the screen we have a French article which you now also have in hard copy entitled "Le Grand Bluff." Sir, is this the article that is the subject of the written statement we just looked at that you gave to the Belgian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I suspect so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we would tender the statement of the witness, 1D5961, I presume MFI to get the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification pending translation. And I take it the article as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would also tender the article. At this point, we have, I believe, the article in all three languages. We would tender it to replace D360, marked not admitted, which was a prior version of the same article before we received the original French. It was an English version that came from the disclosures of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D360. The status will just change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have a short summary to read of the statement, the purpose of which has been explained to the witness yesterday when I met with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness Jan Segers is a Belgian national who served 29 years as a serviceman who has held the rank of lieutenant to commandant. He served for a number of years in a number of military staffs, more specifically in various NATO military headquarters. He was deployed to the former Yugoslavia between 1991 and 1995, firstly as an UNPROFOR officer, and, second, as an UNMO observer. In total, he thinks he spent two and a half years in the former Yugoslavia. He served in Sarajevo, Kiseljak, Bihac, Daruvar, Zagreb, and Kosovo. Mr. Segers recalls an investigation he conducted when two UNMOs were caught and confessed to smuggling money and other things into Bihac out of sympathy for one of the warring factions. They were caught with 50.000 German marks and two mobile phones. Such activity took place sporadically throughout the sector, and the response against it by the UN was very strict. Mr. Segers had information that approximately 10 million German marks were flown in by helicopter into Bihac weekly by the 5th Corps. It went into the hands of Bosnian Muslims in Bihac for weapons and ammunition. One helicopter crashed, and the UNMOs had evidence it was, indeed, a money transport. The witness personally saw a helicopter in Bihac unloading ammunition boxes under the supervision of General Dudakovic. The witness was shot at and arrested by the BiH side for witnessing this. He reported this activity of the ABiH bringing ammunition in helicopters to his UN superiors. He does not know if this was when Bihac was a safe area. Such flights, he agreed, would violate the safe areas agreement. In relation to an interview quoting him as saying: "Without knowing, or without wanting to know, the UN was a source for information for the Croats. This was unacceptable. I know the Americans were supplying them with information, but I think the UN made an unforgivable mistake." Mr. Segers said the term "Americans" was used in a general sense, and he never told the journalist it was about American servicemen; rather, there were consultants hired by various parties. The consulting firm was run by American generals who supported the Croatian army and was staffed with retired American and German officers. Those higher up in the UN hierarchy were advised of this. As to the first Markale market shelling in February 1994, Mr. Segers says that the UN always said it did not know who was responsible but it was almost certain that it was not the Serbs. There were rumours that it was caused by explosives planted under a table, according to what was learned from the report of Military Observers who had visited the market-place after the incident to investigate. He recalled witnessing mortars being fired from Kosevo Hospital, and then the Serbs returned fire, hitting the hospital pavilion complex. When he returned to headquarters, it was said Serbs fired on the hospital. He also said Belgian UNMOs established the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army was regularly shelling a small Bosnian Muslim village simply to get the Americans to carry out bombings. When this was reported, a Pakistani colonel in the UN took the side of the Croats and made threats against the Belgians. Mr. Segers found it outrageous that UN officers took it upon themselves to act as spokesmen for one of the warring factions and to threaten UNMOs who were reporting truthfully. And that is the conclusion of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for answering my questions this morning.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Segers, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Edgerton - you find her to your right - is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Segers.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Segers, if I understood your written evidence correctly, you have been retired from the military for about 15 years now; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm for us, because it's not entirely clear from your written evidence, that you arrived in Sarajevo in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you -- am I correct in my understanding that you left Bosnia in March of 1993 for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I suspect that that's correct, but I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And at what point after you arrived in Sarajevo were you posted to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Bosnia, I was sent to Belgrade for 14 days at first because the UNPROFOR headquarters were still in Belgrade, and then we went from Belgrade to Sarajevo -- excuse me, that's incorrect. We went to Kiseljak, I believe, and then I was posted in the Sarajevo Sector as the liaison officer between the UNPROFOR headquarters in the Sarajevo Sector and the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to map out your time in Bosnia. After you left Sarajevo around March 1993, as you said, you actually never returned to serve in Sarajevo after that; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you weren't in Sarajevo in February 1994 or any other time in 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I suspect that that's correct. I don't have 100 per cent clear view of the exact dates I was present there, but I suspect that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you weren't in Sarajevo on the 28th of June or the 28th of August, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: In 1995, I was not in Sarajevo, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've never met General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I suspect that I met General Mladic once, in Lukavica, during meetings I was conducted at the time with the Serb liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So sometime between October 1992 and March 1993, you had a meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: The meeting is an overstatement. I met him. I never actually had a meeting with him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as a liaison officer, your job is to bring the greatest concerns of UNPROFOR to the attention of the warring factions; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, just speaking about the Bosnian Serb forces, it would have been your job to take concerns to them that related to shelling of civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct. We repeatedly requested cease-fires --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat the last word of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to repeat the last word of your answers. You said you repeatedly requested cease-fires and?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We requested cease-fires on a regular basis. Cease-fires between -- after -- when bombardments were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be that you have used the word "genegotieerd"? That's what I think I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Negotiating" is not entirely the correct word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, did you use that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're telling us that it's not the right expression, and from my understanding of the Dutch, or the Flemish language, "negotiëren" is a Dutch version of "negotiate," "négocier" in French. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was negotiating. Effectively we were the requesting party, so we tried to obtain a decision that was constructive to the request of the UN at that time. So it was a type of negotiating, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in addition, you would have -- in fact, you would make requests and you would bring complaints about just about anything to the Serb side; right? So in addition to shelling, you would bring complaints about the targeting of civilians by sniping. Right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You would bring complaints about restrictions on UNPROFOR's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is something wrong with the microphones. Perhaps you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it was also your job to bring restrictions -- pardon me, to bring complaints about Bosnian Serb army restrictions on UNPROFOR's ability to carry out their humanitarian mission; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't understand the question properly, I think. If you're asking questions about the restrictions of UNPROFOR, would that -- something that we needed to make clear at the time as well, then I can answer that negatively. It wasn't my job, responsibility, at that time to call attention to deficiencies by the UN. It was my job on behalf of the UN [Realtime transcript read in error "UB"] in the Sector Sarajevo and the headquarters of the general at that time for the instructions they gave me which coincided with shooting incidents, shooting between snipers and so on. With the -- to negotiate with the liaison officer from the other side to bring those to an end. And that happened both ways, both towards the Bosnians and toward the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wanted to focus on your interactions with the Bosnian Serb army and those meetings. Now, you mentioned shooting between snipers. My initial question to you about sniping wasn't about shooting between snipers. My question was about the Bosnian Serb army's targeting of civilians. You would -- can you confirm that you would bring complaints about their targeting of civilians by shelling and sniping to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was your liaison interlocutor on the Bosnian Serb army side?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: The problem is that after 20 years, I don't remember the names of the individuals. But there were two Bosnian Serb officers present in the PTT building and I was in contact with them and negotiated with them multiple times a day, and I was sporadically in touch with their head in Lukavica. And, if I'm not mistaken, Lukavica was the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army. But as for the names of the individuals, unfortunately, I have forgotten those.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often would you bring complaints to your interlocutor at Lukavica? And if I can just tell you why I'm asking you this. It's my understanding that the office, the liaison office at the PTT, closed down very early after you arrived in Sarajevo. So I want to know how often after that you went to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. The liaison officer of the Bosnian Serb army in the PTT building was present when I was there, and I consistently negotiated with those people. There were two, at a certain point there were three of them, and then they went back to two. When I mention Lukavica, that was only very sporadically during very serious incidents that I went all the way to Lukavica. But at that point, I had to cross the front line, and sometimes that wasn't possible. So I had to go from the one side to the other side, but there was very intense firing at Sarajevo, and we were -- then we were ineffective. When we were ineffective with the Bosnian Serb liaison officer, then I would try to get to Lukavica, but that was very sporadically. And in my seven months in Sarajevo, the entire period, I went there five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I take from that that when you were at Lukavica and saw General Mladic, it was a very serious shooting incident that prompted your visit?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: My contact with General Mladic was sporadic and very coincidental. It was not in the context of negotiating to achieve a cease-fire or stopping the firing. That was done with the liaison officer, especially with the head liaison officer. Unfortunately, I can't remember the man's name, but it was one of the staff officers of General Mladic. I never personally negotiated with General Mladic about cease-fires at my level.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the word "sporadic." Sporadic means - at least in my understanding - at rare occasions but still more than once. Did you see him, because I do understand you did not meet him, did you see him once or more than once, although only a very few times? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, I met General Mladic a few times, but I never conducted negotiations with him at that point. I can confirm that in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those few times where you met General Mladic between October 1992 and March 1993, was it always at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you ever met General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That does not ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting anybody who represented themselves to be the commander of the Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo subordinate to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible, but my memories at this time are not clear enough about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who typically accompanied General Mladic those times when you met him?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sorry, but I have to say I don't remember that anymore. I don't have any idea. It's vague. I'm not going to make any statements about that because I would be saying something that I cannot confirm with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether or not during those encounters with General Mladic you mentioned that civilians in Sarajevo were being shot and shelled?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: All I can do is return to the fact that I did not conduct any negotiations with General Mladic. I just happened to meet him in the corridor, so there was no real conversation between me and him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I still seek clarification there. You say it wasn't a -- no real conversation. What did you say, Hello, Mr. Mladic, or I'm Mr. Segers. What -- was there any communication at all, or was it just seeing someone in passing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was escorted by the head liaison officer of the Serb army at the time. I don't remember the man's name anymore. And in the corridor, General Mladic was passing. We passed General Mladic and were introduced to each other but that was it. There was no follow-up. It was just a courtesy introduction of both individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How were you introduced to each other? Is this Mr. Segers, liaison for UNPROFOR, or just a name? What happened exactly, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, it was: This is Mr. Segers, he is one of the liaison officers from the UNPROFOR headquarters. And I was told, This is General Mladic, may I introduce you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how was General Mladic introduced to you? Did they say what his position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, they told me, This is the commander. And when they said "the commander," I knew that was General Mladic. I don't actually remember the name Mladic being stated. I remember being told he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you knew his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did not know the face of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. General Galic does not ring any bells automatically, so I can't really connect that with anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a liaison officer, the name of General Galic didn't mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this time, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your prior question didn't make it into the transcript because the translation was continuing, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I should have been -- let me see. I think I said: As a liaison officer, the name of General Galic didn't mean anything to you. If that's the question which you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me look at the other one. I think what is missing ... I have asked, and I don't know whether that's what is missing, whether the witness knew the face of General Mladic and I asked similar question, whether he was aware of what General Galic looked like. I think that may be what is missing. And I think the witness told us that he knew the face of General Mladic and he, as far as matters stand now, that he does not -- that he did not know or at least doesn't remember, at this moment, whether he knew the face of General Galic at the time. And I'm sorry for complicating matters by direct listening. I'm now better aware of what problems you may face now and then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I might come back to this, but for the moment I want to move forward, so because of -- it seems to me, because of your job and because you were based in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, you should have been able to see something about the situation for civilians there. So I want to ask you about that. Now, in the published interview from November 1995 in Télé Moustique you said when you arrived in Sarajevo, you found women and children had become the targets of an army, the Bosnian Serb army. So am I right in understanding that refers to what you saw; right? You saw obvious civilians being shot by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you saw these people also being shot while they were doing civilian things, just their normal everyday business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just putting ourselves in October 1992 for a moment, when you arrived in Sarajevo, you would have recalled that most of the Bosnian-held city had no water and no electricity; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So part of the everyday business for civilians at that time because of these privations would mean they would have to go outside and find water and food; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when they were going out trying to find water and food, sometimes that could take hours because it was so restricted; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is very, very much correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- and when they were trying to find water and food, people would get killed and wounded by Bosnian Serb sniping or shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct, to the extent that, of course, where you're referring to the shooting at the point where the water was by the Serbians, well, that is different version through the Military Observers that were doing the crater analysis there on site where -- whereas, you know, for the other facts I'll confirm it, but not for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have actually no idea what specific water line incident you're talking about. I'm just asking you more general questions about the situation for civilians in Sarajevo. What -- so what you saw was people being driven outdoors by privations, and while they were outside of their homes, they were targeted by shelling and sniping; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while they were outside -- and because -- because people were shot and shelled while they were outside, and because you were in the city to see this, you must have seen that everybody had this kind of obsessive fear that they might be the next casualty of the shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll object at this point as it asked the witness to make speculation as to what was in other people's minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, another matter is it's a rather composite question. You introduce a few things, so would you please split it up and refrain where possible from what the witness couldn't know by himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, based in the city as you were, did you have an opportunity to talk with the civilian residents of the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recall them sharing some of their experiences with you about their daily life?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct. And this was the case with all inhabitants of Sarajevo, the various ethnic groups, because I spoke both to Serb and Bosnian and Croatian civilians in Sarajevo, and their fate or their destiny at the time seemed to be the same for all of them. It was unpleasant, it was dangerous. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as a result of -- or during the course of those conversations, do you recall the city's civilian residents speaking about their state of mind?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yeah, affirmative. And the people were living under this panicked fear continually and it was -- well, let's say that that was sort of more or less what people told me, We can be shot at at any minute now. We don't feel safe. The danger is coming from the sky or the buildings just opposite us. So, yes, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, because of your job, you would also have been aware of the shelling pattern or practices of the Bosnian Serb army, in terms of their mortars and artillery; right? You would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I saw the shootings of Sarajevo several times, and I know very well what mortar fire is because several years I commanded a mortar unit, and so, yes, I have expertise in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would have seen that shells were fired in a way that was widely dispersed across the populated areas of the entire city, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Effectively, yes, I had that same impression. Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have seen also that that shelling was -- that widely dispersed shelling wasn't typically related to an obvious military target or front-line military activity; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you a two-fold answer. In that regard usually you would be right. Effectively, it is a sort of wild firing. However, I also saw outcoming fire from the centre of Sarajevo to the Kosevo Hospital, for example, where afterwards naturally the Serbians had a targeted counter-attack. So it wasn't just always widely disseminated fire, but, yes, generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk for a minute about the Kosevo Hospital incident that you discussed in your written evidence. So, first of all, the hospital is actually, as you remember, a really large compound in the north-east part of the city, right, with many different clinics or buildings?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you said you heard two explosions and you looked out of a window and saw two mortars had been fired, you were -- that means you were inside one of the buildings of the compound when you saw that; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct. I made my observation from the building. There were various pavilions and between the pavilions there were two mortars set up. And I didn't just think they fired, I saw them effectively fire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to sit back from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, a couple of my colleagues, the interpreters, have asked if you could just sit back from the microphone a little bit, maybe right where you are now, so that they could hear you clearly. So just talking about these mortars. You've said the Serbs retaliated. Now, they retaliated sometime after you saw that fire; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as I understand your written evidence, they didn't hit the mortars. They hit one of the buildings of the hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I know that they retaliated, fired on the building, but the story is a bit longer. It's not I fire, I fire back. It was outgoing fire from Bosnian -- well, the Muslim army first, from Sarajevo to the Serb positions, and then the Serbian or liaison officer brought complaints to us, but I wasn't there, my colleague counted them, and said, That would have to stop or we will defend ourselves, we are entitled to that. We'll fire back. And then effectively, after a while and at -- at that time the mortars of the Bosnian Muslim army had already departed or had been taken away, I should say, there was a shooting, a short shelling of the hospital really without there being any material substantive damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it wasn't just five minutes as you -- as was printed in the Télé Moustique article. There was kind of a greater expanse of time that allowed for this communication with the Serbian LO; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But how long was this interval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, the question had been clearly asked for another five minutes. We'll give you another five minutes and then we'll fire back. And this was the time they spoke to my colleague liaison officer, a Norwegian fellow, who was present at the PTT building, where I was at the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly that at the time when this retaliatory firing took place, the mortar that had been at the Kosevo Hospital had already moved away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never spoke of casualties. What happened is that the mortars, so the weapons that had been used by the Bosnian Muslim army, that they had already been removed from that location. I didn't speak of casualties or victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I didn't ask about casualties either. Thank you, Madam Edgerton. You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, I'm looking at the clock as well. At this point in time, Mr. Segers, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back soon. I have one technical matter, that is, the French version of the article. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To attach it to D360 might not be fully accurate because D360 is the English version of the article but not as a translation of the article, but it's an UNPROFOR document which states where it was published, et cetera. Now it may be very practical to nevertheless attach it to it, not being exclusively a translation where the English has two or three lines more, but it seems very practical to do that. At the same time, the translation in the UNPROFOR document, is that a verified one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honours. But we do have a CLSS translation of the French article. I intended to tender the French article, the CLSS translation into both B/C/S and English, in lieu of the current D360 MNA which was not admitted precisely because of the flaws in the language that Your Honour noted when we only had that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, what we now have, that is, the UNPROFOR document with a translation which contains most of the text of the article, should then be replaced by new versions. Now, the B/C/S translation, is that done on the basis of the UNPROFOR English or is it done on the basis of the English translation of the French original? Because there's another source of potential errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I would suggest to the parties the following, that for the time being, that we replace D360, the UNPROFOR original, English version, that we replace that by 1D05960, I think it is, and that then the B/C/S translation will be verified on the basis of the -- of the French original. So that we have the French original and we have then two translations, one directly taken from the French into English and not the UNPROFOR one which is not verified, and then a B/C/S translation being verified on the basis of the French original and not being a translation of the English UNPROFOR version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, there's just another little twist to that, and I apologise. But D360 was actually shown to Witness Butler and he testified on the basis of that document. So I would suggest leaving D360 intact, but assigning 1D05960, which is what Your Honours have been discussing, a new D number and then taking those steps that Your Honour has suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would avoid further complications because we wouldn't know what Mr. Butler testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But we wouldn't because it's MNA, it's marked not admitted, so we would not have a record of what Mr. Butler was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if is marked for identification, at least we would know what was shown to him. We should then change the status in marked for identification, but I think that's status a document cannot bear forever. I think -- I invite the parties to resolve the matter together with the Registrar and that we ensure that at least what was shown to Mr. Butler is still known to those who are studying the record, that finally that we also have the original -- the -- the English version therefore should -- should remain somewhere, then the French version and the new English translation of that one and the B/C/S translation of that one should be available as well. I don't think that we get major problems with it in the future, but if you would please discuss that with Mr. Registrar, what's the best way to have a complete record on this matter. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for the witness, I can present what we believe is the course of action for the documents we discussed before the break. We have confirmed that D360 MNA, the original bad English, I'll call it, copy from UNPROFOR, was shown to several witnesses in addition to Mr. Butler. Therefore it should probably retain a separate status and separate position in e-court. We have thus agreed to then have 1D05960 be marked for identification as a separate D number given that we have also confirmed the B/C/S was a translation of the bad English D360 MNA rather than the original French or the English translation of the original French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore it should be marked for identification as well so -- and then we should wait until we have verified English and B/C/S translations for the two -- for -- for the French original. Yes. And that should be under a new number then, although I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number, Mr. Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1D5960 will be MFI D1466.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D1466 with a huge exclamation mark reference should be -- a link should be made to the -- to D360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you tell us whether the status of MNA could be changed in marked for identification and again ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be done as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Segers, we'll continue. Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, just staying with the subject of the Kosevo Hospital that we left off with, I'd like to ask you this. Because of your job, the position you were in, and the fact that you were stationed in the city, you can confirm that during your tour, in fact, the Kosevo Hospital was repeatedly heavily shelled by Bosnian Serb mortars and artillery; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And -- and what you were telling us was about the one time you were there on the spot when something like that happened.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct. I referred to that because I was effectively present there and did not hear it based on rumours or hearsay. I experienced that. What I repeatedly encountered during my period in Sarajevo was that certain points such as UN buildings were used to position artillery or mortar and to fire from there. The same happened at the PTT building, for example. And, of course, the Serb adversaries retaliated. And I'm talking about the Kosevo because I effectively saw it, I was present there, I am not basing this on rumours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned just before we broke that you had commanded a mortar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to firing from UN positions. As a liaison officer, did you in any way deal with that? Did you complain with the Bosnian -- Bosnian army or -- what was your role? And do you remember how it was reported, what was reported? Because we have some evidence about these kind of incidents, and I just want to find out whether that's about the same or whether this adds to what we have received already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shelling that took place from firing outgoing from Sarajevo and was sometime in the immediate surroundings of the building, not from the actual UN building but from the surroundings, there was regular firing, and then the Serb side would react to us as liaison officers. And we would report that and talk to the Muslim liaison officers and we would make clear that the situation could not continue. Generally, we would receive a positive response, and they would cease firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you two questions. First of all, how often, as far as you remember, did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a difficult question. I remember vaguely multiple incidents. I was there for seven months, as I said. In memory, I recall four or five cases that I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have received evidence about firing in the -- near to the UN positions. Do I understand you well that what you initially said is that it was from the UN positions, that that's not correct but that was close by UN positions that fire --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. It was from nearby the positions. I remember that they had to remain at least 200 metres away from the UN positions and that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and what was the closest and what -- if you remember? I mean, 180 metres is also within 200 metres but not the same as 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't matter. It was even against the building that they would position a tank to fire. So I can't quantify it in metres but it was -- without any debate it was within the 200-metre zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just also ask a question. Sir, you confirmed to Madam Edgerton a few minutes ago that the Kosevo Hospital was repeatedly heavily shelled by Bosnian Serb mortars and artillery. You remember that? That was at page 26, line 22 to 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. I -- I remember that I said that. Now I'm getting back to what I just said. Like most of us, I was regularly notified about shelling of the hospital. I saw shelling of the hospital, and once I saw outgoing fire when I was present. That's what I wanted to mention in that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you've told us that. I just want to ask you about the several times that the Kosevo Hospital was heavily shelled. In those instances apart from the one that you witnessed when you were at the hospital yourself, had there been a provocative shooting from the hospital or was it just shelling of the hospital without any provocation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to answer that. I suspect that there was. The evidence that there was provocation -- provocative shooting from the hospital is what I'd mentioned, but I can't confirm every single incident that that is said to have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. You confirmed that there was provocative shooting on the one occasion when you were at the hospital yourself. I'm asking you about other instances when the shelling took place. Now you say you suspect. You haven't got any information that, in fact, that was so. It's just your suspicion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I can't confirm that it was provocative in the other cases. I can't confirm that. What I can say, as I just illustrated with another example about the surroundings of the PTT building where they positioned a tank and the Serb retaliatory firing, you always have the same scenario: We'll give you five minutes to stop, and if not, we'll fire back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Let's not confuse the PTT with the Kosevo. I'm specifically talking about the Kosevo Hospital. So that you don't have any information that the ABiH had fired before the other shelling took place by the Serb side except for the one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Segers, before we broke, you mentioned that you had commanded a mortar unit in the past. So I'd like to ask you this: Having been a commander, you would know about the potential for different settings to be used on the projectile, super-quick, quick, and delay, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And super-quick detonates immediately on impact; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct. Super-quick is an explosion that happens immediately upon impact on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you can use a quick or delay setting on the projectile so that it has the potential to penetrate a building before it explodes; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: There are three possible explosions: An air explosion which can take place in the air before it impacts the ground, there is an immediate impact explosion on the ground, and there's the delayed explosion. In these cases, the most serious damage would be caused by the first two options, so the air explosion and the immediate impact on ground one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my question is actually specific to the settings on the projectile, and it was whether you can use a quick or a delay setting -- or let me rephrase. Asking you to confirm that a quick or delay setting on the projectile is something you can use so that the projectile penetrates the building before it explodes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now I'd like to show you a document, and it's from the time of your tour, 65 ter number 15760. And it's going to show up on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I think there might not be a B/C/S translation, so I'll read slowly what I need -- oh, there is. Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is UNMO Carl Harding's report to the Senior Military Observer for Sarajevo, dated January 2nd, 1993, on battle damage to Kosevo Hospital and the effects of that damage on the hospital's operation. And that's what the squadron leader says in the first paragraph. And paragraph 2 talks about the casualty reception building and its structure and its layout. And then, with your leave, we can turn the page, if you've had enough of a look at this, and I want to direct you to a part that I want to ask you a question about. Is it -- all right. Now, I want us to go down and look at paragraph 4, and it says there that: The third (top) floor of the casualty reception building has had several direct hits by 122-millimetre artillery and 40-millimetre anti-aircraft gun. A partly detonated artillery round was observed which was reported to have impacted on 20 December 1992. The fuse setting was on Q, which is quick, with the other settings of SQ, super-quick, and delay clearly being seen. Other impacts at this level may well be from tank fire due to size and penetration. So, first of all, you know that a tank is -- a tank projectile is a direct-fire weapon; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what -- now back to the document. What Squadron Leader Harding is reporting is a mortar projectile that's set to penetrate a building; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: What I can infer from this is that when it is set at quick, we'll get a normal explosion. Meaning when it impacts the objective, it takes about 1 or 1 and a half seconds to explode. But that's not actual penetration through the building and then exploding with a delay system. And this refers to quick and super-quick. Those are two systems that are not set to the delay system with a penetration purpose. Because the delay won't cause the explosion until it's penetrated -- the -- the wall. Here we have the quick or super-quick, so I'm not sure whether they had the option of using the delay setting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that this be admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object since the -- there has been no foundation laid for any knowledge of the witness as to the specific events that are recalled in this document. The Prosecution has had ample time to present their case and has had ample time to present bar table documents. They have chosen not to submit this earlier. They therefore cannot now at this point in time submit it when it's not related to the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How is it -- I'm not sure how it's unrelated to the testimony of the witness, Your Honour. The witness has said he can commanded a mortar unit, so he has some knowledge about mortars. The witness has confirmed that the Kosevo Hospital was repeatedly shelled during his tour. And I'm asking him about a specific example of that. And perhaps I've moved to tender the document a little too early, Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did he say he was a commander of a mortar unit in examination-in-chief or cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In cross-examination, Your Honours. In responding to this, I asked him questions about this document, and this was new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the objection is denied. In the evidence of the witness, there is an issue of responding to provocative fire from the Kosevo Hospital. Now, the type of fire at the Kosevo Hospital may be relevant to understand whether this was in response to provocation or not, and to that extent, it deals with matters which were raised in examination-in-chief. The objection therefore is denied. Please proceed. Yes, I mean, please proceed, answer the question. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you tendered the document, I'm -- I apologise. Mr. Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 15760 will be Exhibit P7823, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were -- you were repeatedly notified of the shelling, the heavy shelling, of Kosevo Hospital. In fact, the shelling of the hospital was a matter of such concern that the commander raised it with the Bosnian Serb leadership. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: As far as I understand, yes. But if you say the commanders, it could be General Morillon at the UNPROFOR level. It could also be Colonel Valentin, who, at the time, was the commander of the Sarajevo Sector. And I think in this case, it would have been the commander of the Sarajevo Sector who would be conversing with the main authorities from the Serbs just as they did with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact -- and we can have a look at another document, 65 ter number 33763. This is an UNPROFOR report to SMO, Senior Military Observer, Sector Sarajevo, about the shelling of the Kosevo Hospital on 29, 30, and 31 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to English and B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see there a report from Major Vesselov to the Senior Military Observer just one month after the document we just looked at that says that Kosevo Hospital's premises received 11 mortar impacts within the space of about two hours, causing damage to the cardiology clinic and the orthopaedic surgery. The most probable area of fire being south of Donji Mrkovici. That's the last line of this report. And if you go over to English and B/C/S page 3, you see the next UNMO's report referring to the shelling of the 29th of January, saying at paragraph 2 that the greatest damage of the shelling on that day was done by a 155-millimetre shell, which, in summary, entered a room, continued along the floor, and then ricochetted into another room. So these are the severe incidents that you were informed of in the ordinary course of your business; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, I do need to call your attention to the fact that I was not a Military Observer at this point. I was liaison officer between the warring factions. So from the Military Observers via the Sector Sarajevo or the UNPROFOR headquarters, I had to be tasked to negotiate a cease-fire. What you're referring to, there's a clear difference between 155-millimetres, then we talk about artillery fire. When we talk about 122-millimetre fire, which you showed in the previous document, that's mortar fire. Artillery has a fire higher effective firing capacity, and it's far more punctual than mortar fire. The purpose of an artillery shelling -- the target is far -- it is usually far more accurate than mortar firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about whether -- or you mentioned that these issues would be raised either by General Morillon or General Valentin with the Bosnian Serb leadership. So could we -- before --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter number 33796.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a letter of protest by General Morillon to Dr. Karadzic dated - and there's no B/C/S translation, I think - dated 31 January 1993, saying: To my distress, I've just been informed that Kosevo Hospital has today been the target of some shelling by Serb artillery or mortars. Noting that at 3.00 p.m. a shell hit a part of the hospital and injured two patients, two staff, a journalist, and a doctor, and lodging a strong protest, in fact, protest, in his words, in the strongest terms for this irresponsible attack and says that there can be no excuse for shelling a hospital. So, Mr. Segers, General Morillon's referring to the attack that we just talked about in this document, the document we just looked at, the UNMO report, and the -- which included artillery fire on the hospital. So what General Morillon is protesting is the direct targeting of the hospital building, right, or a building in the hospital, right? I see you nodding but you'll have to say something eventually so it can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to your knowledge, even after this time-period, the hospital continued to be targeted by Bosnian Serb mortars and artillery, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: There was certainly another shelling after 31 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have these two documents, 65 ter 33763 and 33796, as Prosecution exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 33763 will Exhibit P7824. And 65 ter 33796 will be Exhibit P7825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And translation of the last one, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First one is I think you said there was a translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, but the second one not. So the second one should be marked for identification, of course, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P7824 is admitted into evidence. P7825 is marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I want to move and talk about a couple of things that you referred to in the published interview that appeared in Télé Moustique, and that's, first of all, with respect to the first market-place shelling. And I just want to say, since we noticed that the interview was published in November 1995 -- or I just want to ask, since we noticed that the interview was published in November 1995, that only, I take it, reflects some information you had or information you had as of that time. It's not necessarily a complete picture of anything, and I'm talking particularly about these events in Sarajevo after March 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So with respect to the first market-place shelling, you said in the published interview, and I'll read it exactly, that: The UN still maintains that it was -- that it's not known who was responsible, however, we are almost certain that it was not the Serbs. And then you said: There are certain rumours that an explosive device had been placed under a table. And then you said in the procès-verbal of your interview in Belgium that that statement I've just quoted was based on a report of Military Observers who'd visited the market-place immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you said on "a report." I think what the witness said in his statement was on "the report" of the Military Observers, which is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a great deal of evidence in this trial from -- and other trials at this organisation from serving and former UN officials, including former UNMOs, who were involved in the investigation about what caused this blast, and we've not seen any UNMO --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My friend is on his feet, so perhaps I better stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was waiting until he would start objecting, but that he was about to do such a thing was clear to me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only part that I have a problem with is making reference to evidence from other trials. I don't think that's appropriate to be referencing evidence from other trials that may not be in evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps, Ms. Edgerton, it would have been appropriate to say that there are also adjudicated facts, which, of course, come from other trials, but this Chamber received information that's from this and from other trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've not seen any UNMO or other UN report that refers to that blast being caused by a static explosion. So my question for you is: You don't have a copy of any report or the report that you say you based this statement on, do you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: No. I don't have a copy, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you done with that or ... I see that you're turning the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Probably, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Probably. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it was the report of the Military Observers from which you got this information. When did you see that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mention a report, to the extent that I can remember it because a lot of years have passed, we were notified about the shelling incident, not shelling, the explosion on the market-place and possible shelling via CNN. We had -- we were watching CNN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Apparently you're now talking about other sources of knowledge. Does that mean that you don't have a clear recollection of a, or the, report of Military Observers describing that who -- who most likely fired that shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The report was merely an oral report I received from MOs returning from inspection and crater analysis. There was never any written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether there never were any, you haven't seen one, I take it? That's what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you tell us where were you when this was reported to you orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in my office with my colleague, and we immediately followed up on the incident and contacted the Military Observers to ask them what they knew about it. And that's how we received additional information and started to question whether it was a shelling after having heard what was on CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking already some questions which were not yet put to you. You were, you said, in your office. Where was that office at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was for Markale I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. The name Markale I doesn't ring a bell. Markale I is shellings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are talking here ... let me just check. I think you were asked about a shelling of a market where ... rumours would have it that a static explosive was put under one of the stalls. Is that the Markale market where 60 people died that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said you received --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't get the translation of his answer and therefore it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat my answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said I think "affirmative."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what we -- and I'm looking at the parties, what we usually refer to as Markale I, unless there's any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We do, but obviously to someone in the field it may not have been Markale I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you remember -- you said you were in the office at the PTT building. Do you remember when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven months after I arrived. So let me think back because it's been so long ago. So it's difficult for me to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I now move to a different channel in order to avoid that I speak and put my next question before the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you have answered the question. Now, you said that you were informed about the shelling, and you heard that when you were in the PTT building in your office. And I think you also told us that you left Sarajevo in -- well, first half of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the first half of 1993, I suspect so. I don't have a clear impression of that, but it corresponds with my total presence being seven months in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you in Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now move to the English channel in order to avoid that I'm missing that some translation, whether it's Dutch or English or French, has not yet been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, now it's your question that wasn't caught so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was: Were you in Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, no, as far as I can think, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware that this Chamber received a lot of evidence which always situates this incident in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. I can't confirm that. You have that evidence. I can only say that I have vague suspicions or we may be talking about two different things. However, the entire matter of the shelling there, that caused a number of casualties is -- or what I thought were -- were 60 casualties that in the market-place shelling, that that's how I recall it and that the story that I gave you about this was at the -- it was at the time when I was in my position in -- in the position of liaison officer at the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this oral report you received, as you've said, have you ever seen any written report about the incident you are describing which caused 60 casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not see a written report. What did happen is that on my later assignments when I was in Zagreb working as an MIO, so Military Information Officer, of the Military Observers, I had a colleague who was an English SAS officer, and he -- and I saw this at one time as well, a copy of a code cable that had been sent to New York and in which that story was related, that this was not a shelling, but in all likelihood, indeed, it had concerned an explosive device that had been placed below a table and I read as much. And we -- and that was confirmed to me and we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you're still talking about a cable that dealt with an incident where some 60 people had died where the explosive device may have been placed below a table. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you speak of cable, we here mean code cable and that is a coded message between -- right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that coded cable dealt with the incident you referred to in your interview, talking about the -- the incident where 60 people had died and where it was said that it may have been an explosive device, a static explosive device, under a table. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm seeking the assistance of the parties, of a market-place incident, shelling, with 60 dead people, because it sounds to some extent as Markale I. At the same time, I'm getting confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Without being accused of trying to offer any information to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We are at a time anyhow --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For a break, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where we would take a break anyhow and perhaps we take that break very soon and then I will receive further information from you. A few follow-up questions. The information you said you received orally, you received it from whom or from what team or group of people? Could you be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that information which I received at the time came from the Military Observers, Sector Sarajevo, so the Military Observers in that a sector with whom I had immediate direct radio contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You received it by radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of a person who gave you that you oral report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, to my great regret, I do not. It's too long ago. I don't have the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they say that almost for certain the shell had been fired by the Muslims rather than by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They said that there could not be a thorough crater analysis because, according to them, no artillery had been fired. And so they spoke -- they said the conclusion of their research was that it was an explosive device, but that was their initial conclusion at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you hear of any follow-up conclusions in the days following?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. What I heard further was that effectively the Serbs had shot the market-place, but this was counter to what that initial observation had been by the Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And where is that presented in your interview, that after the initial report that it would not have been the Serbs, that later on you were informed that it was shelling by the Serbs? Have you mentioned that in your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did indeed say this to the man who took my interview; and, of course, he didn't include this integrally, fully in his text. But, yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think at the end of the interview you were asked whether you had read it, and then the next question was whether you wished to add or improve anything, and that's what we find in the semi-last page of the interview. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I do not wish to add or improve anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- if I may make a suggestion, you've been using the term "interview," whereas we have two interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I meant, of course, your statement you gave in Belgium, not to a newspaper, but in the presence of an examining magistrate. There you said that had you read it and that there was nothing you would like to add. Do you consider it relevant for this Court to know that your initial report, oral report, that it were mostly not likely the Serbs, would you consider it relevant for us to know that reports later on gave a pretty different opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, that would be relevant for the Court to know. All I can do is -- is, you know, get back to what I was told and what I remembered and what I even today consider to have been an objective report immediately by the people that I had faith in, the Military Observers who were permanently on the terrain and who were first on the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what they told you after further investigations, after one, two, or three days, you considered that not to be reliable any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hard to say. I always ask myself is this simply something that they wanted to -- to disguise, you know, be very secret about, about this operation. But that is such a personal interpretation that I would have to sort of push that away from me. I had such faith, however, in these people that I thought that what they were saying was indeed correct. However, you know, perhaps at the time this was not something that was popular to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they said two things, if we understand you well. One day, they say A; a few days later, they say B. And was it that you made up for yourself what to believe and then introduce that in your -- giving your statement in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative, yeah. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
