utterances.text: Then my question is: Is that the whole truth, or is it the part of the truth which you considered to be most reliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me, it is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the fact that two, three days later, they came with a different view, you do not consider that to be part of the truth which you should tell this Court, because whether they were right or wrong, that's what they told you two or three days later, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that. Yes, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I want to take you back to your statement on page 9. Today you said the report was an oral report by these Military Observers and that there was no written report that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Insofar as I can recall, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the middle of that page in your statement, I find a sentence and I would like to ask you to explain it: "I wish to remark that the French text says that we were 'almost certain' that it was not the Serbs." This is the sentence I find in your statement. French text? How do I understand have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is just orally quoting what the Military Observers had told me at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it a text, the oral report, is it a text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was an oral report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then it's at least not entirely precise to say it was the French text. There was no text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps I misunderstood you. Where I spoke of French text, then are you quoting the interview? I was not given a text by the Military Observers. We had a talk, as I said, and so, effectively, almost certain is a correct interpretation of that oral report given me by the Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please have D1465 on the screen, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's page 8 in the Dutch, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the gentleman doesn't actually have the hard copies of these two documents in front of him. Just a suggestion to try and be helpful, maybe if my friend could give him the hard copies that were prepared of his interview in Belgium and the published interview from 1995, that might help him clarify some of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe the hard copies are still with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 9 in the English and page 8, as Mr. Ivetic told us, in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the bottom of the page in Dutch beginning with the number 20. That's the question, I believe, that Your Honours is focusing on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a bit confusing, but I would like to clarify that. In -- under number 20, we have your answer: "The information presented there was based on what I had learned from a report of the Military Observers who had visited the market-place immediately after the incident with the intention of finding out who had caused the explosion." That was your answer. And then the next sentence which follows reads, I quote: "I wish to remark that the French text says that we were 'almost certain' that it was not the Serbs." What do you mean by "French text"? That is all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French text, well, as far as I can interpret from what I have before me here, is simply the interview that was done with me by the journalist of that magazine. And so I believe, as far as I know, the textual quote is what I gave him and what the military -- and that what was the Military Observers had said to me, and the report was not in French. It was, in fact, in English, but I simply repeated to the journalist the words that I had heard from the observers and they had said "almost certainly." And as you're quoting it here "grande certitude," nearly certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the matter. When you say now said it was not in French, it was, in fact, in English, then you are referring to the oral report of the Military Observers you received? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would still have, before we take the break, a short follow-up question, unless there's something that needs clarification, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to alleviate any confusion to those who are not fluent in the language, the Dutch statement also has French text that is not translated in the English version that follows the Dutch. That was the procedure that we had in place and that French text is the original French from the article, the interview with Télé Moustique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you were also asked about the rumours about explosive under a table. First of all, did those who reported to you officially - so not rumours, but those who came or reported to you perhaps even by radio - did they state that there would have been a static explosive under a table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. And that was the first report that I got from them and also the one that remained in my mind, that oral report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received some evidence about crater analysis of what was found on that market. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think they must have based themselves on something, I suppose, in the end to come to that statement that the Serbs had shot. And I stick to my position that that was the first information that I got from the Military Observers, very briefly, after the facts that that was correct -- well, you know the story that I just told you. And they said at the time that there could not be a clear crater analysis. They didn't say that they wouldn't do a crater analysis. They didn't say -- they said they couldn't do a crater analysis that would clearly show that the Serbs had shot. So -- but they weren't -- they didn't negate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in one of your earlier answers today I think you said they were not talking about a crater analysis because there was no impact on the ground or at least something of the kind, if it was a static explosive, there was no way to even do a crater analysis. Do I now understand that they hinted at least at a possible -- possibility of, perfect or imperfect, crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military Observers in an area just after a shelling or shooting would always initially do a crater analysis. So, in principle, that would be one of their immediate duties. And they reported to me that at the time crater analysis was a problem and that they could not do a clear crater analysis, which is not to say that there weren't, you know, any -- any shards -- or no, not shards but traces of an explosive on the ground. But that's not really a true crater analysis. And I don't know what your Court has in terms of evidence but I never saw it. I can only come back what I said all along, that immediately after the fact they reported to me that a crater analysis would be a problem and so they could not conclude that the Serbs had, in fact, fired, and it was more likely to them that there had been a static explosive device below a table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're using the expression "more likely," and not "almost certain." Any explanation for that difference in language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really see any difference. For me, more likely, well, almost certain is stronger, but what I remember initially that almost certainly it was that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they tell you at that time on what basis they thought it might have been a static explosive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion about what would have been the basis for such an opinion, that it may have been a static explosive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I formed an opinion about that. What struck me at that point was that when the first rumours started arriving about the explosion, we sent the first specialists to the site to know exactly what had happened. And at that point already, as I said before, CNN was saying worldwide that the Serbs had shot at the market, had shelled the market. What surprised me at the time, because no investigation had been conducted yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're answering a question which I did not put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about the background of what CNN reported. I was asking you about what the basis was for an opinion, or the opinion, that it may have been a static device that exploded. On what basis was that expressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed of that by the Military Observers who, at the time, were convinced that that was a possible answer, and they were continuing on that basis, based on the traces on the ground from the explosion. Not much else was said about that at the time. It was all very brief and happened in very rapid succession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the basis for the opinion which was reported to you, that it may have been a static explosive, was what they found on the spot, as far as traces are concerned. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correctly put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I refer to your statement given in Belgium in the presence of the Defence, where you were asked: "Who was, according to the rumours, responsible for putting an explosive under a table?" And you answered that you would not answer that question. Here it is rumours which is at the basis of the opinion that it may have been a static explosive, not what was reported as the result of the initial investigation. Could you explain why, when you were asked about who, according to the rumours, was responsible, and when you were asked what the source of those rumours were, that you didn't wish to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had and I still have partial immunity from the UN and that was the context in which I did not want to answer the questions because I knew the polemic that would ensue, and I was trying to avoid a polemic. Especially because this concerned, as far as I was told and I was also convinced of this, and this somewhere conflicted with the official statements by the UN. That's the reason that I didn't want to answer at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't say, I don't want to answer questions. You left the impression that it was rumours. And now you could have clarified that by giving clear answers; that is, it was on the basis of the initial investigation that they came to this opinion. But you preferred to avoid any revealing of contradictions and official statements, and you made your own choices in what you considered relevant to tell us and what you considered not relevant to tell us, even when it was only a part of the truth. That's where we are, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All I can do is confirm what I keep saying and that will stand to the facts or rumours. There was an official communication. To what extent is that a rumour, is it being refuted by other facts, all I can say, okay, that happened too, that happened in addition, but it doesn't refute the first facts. And the first facts most certainly were communicated by institution observing on site directly to the liaison officer who communicates that as the liaison and who, of course, has to be aware to have the shelling stop in time to start negotiations at the instruction of a higher authority at the point. So what bothers me is that people are saying, Are you basing this on rumours. In retrospect, perhaps they were rumours, but I don't assume that. To me, it was an objective account of the facts by the professional team onsite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, contradicted three days later by that same team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that, but that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that for the time being. But, once again, you were not in Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have my diary with me, and I would have to check my diary. No, but I don't think so. That seems ... I performed various assignments in the Balkans, at least seven different assignments, and as far as I can remember, I was not in Sarajevo at the time, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. You may follow the usher and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps my recollection doesn't serve me sufficiently, but if any of the parties could point at where there's anything in evidence other than what we are familiar with as Markale I dealing with 60 casualties and an insinuation of a static explosive under a table and immediately an UNMO report on the matter, then this Chamber would like to know so that we are better able to evaluate the evidence of this witness and perhaps finds a link to an event which may have escaped my mind at this very moment. There was another matter, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The matter I did not want to raise in front of the witness was precisely this. Paragraph 20 gives a date for the incident that he is talking about, and one could show that to him and see if that refreshes his recollection. This paragraph 20 indicates that the incident he is talking about is in February 1994, which would make it the Markale that we have been -- that we talk about as Markale I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I more or less acted on the basis of the description of the event, but there's no -- perhaps Ms. Edgerton could ask the witness because it's a matter which may be more for cross-examination than ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The paragraph says 70 people were killed, not 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think 60 has been mentioned as well and -- or over 60. I think that's a detail -- we are talking about far beyond 50. Whether that's 60 or 70. We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, since another witness is still waiting, could you give us an impression on how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have two areas left to cover. I figure at the speed we're going, it would take 20 minutes at best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right now, I think 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's close to one session. Perhaps we could make this session slightly shorter and then have the witness who was interrupted to be here for the last session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Judge Fluegge, has another question for you Mr. Segers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to fully understand your previous answers before the break, on page 52, lines 10 to 12, you said, I quote: "And they reported to me that at the time crater analysis was a problem and that they could not do a clear crater analysis ..." And then one page later, page 53, lines 10 and 11, you said: "... we sent the first specialists to the site to know exactly what had happened." Is my understanding correct that you first received this oral report, it was too dangerous to carry out a specific and proper crater analysis, and because of that you sent later the first specialists to the site to make that analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that last part is not correct, since, you know, we did not send the Military Observers. They went on their own initiative to locations, but there was a permanent standing order that they would go to the terrain immediately and then do a crater analysis to ascertain who had done the shooting. They were the specialists, in that entirety of people present from the UN, they were specialists in crater analysis and therefore were a point of reference for us. And I got in touch with them as soon as I received the information over the news, and they then told me they were on site but could not come to an objective decision that there had been a Serbian shooting. But as I say, this was tied to the information that I was given orally at the time, that I was getting in at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's still unclear, in my view. You said, page 53: "Yes, of course, I formed an opinion about that. What struck me at that point was that when the first rumours started arriving about the explosion, we sent the first specialists to the site to know exactly what had happened." I don't know what you mean by "we sent." Did you send specialist or -- you and your colleagues or the UN or whoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are the UN in this case, so the specialists of the UN who go on location as the first, and they were specialists, not one, it was an entire team, and that team went to the site, this team of Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did you receive a report from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I recall is that that was the oral report of which I speak. I do not recall that there was a written report which did not necessarily have to go through me, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to go onto something that you discussed in the published interview, and in the original it's at page 4 on the top right-hand side and you mentioned in your procès-verbal. It's the market attack that, as you said, preceded the massive NATO raids against the Serbs. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we're going to refer to the procès-verbal, I think it's fair to give the position in the procès-verbal so that the witness and everyone can find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. English and Flemish page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in respect of that shelling, you said: "The UNMO who investigated immediately after the catastrophe as well as several UNMO officers stated that it was likely the shell had been fired by the Muslims." And in question 21b of your procès-verbal, you were asked: "What's your knowledge based on?" And you said: "On the report of the Military Observers." One of those specialists you were just talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My friend is standing up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the question to the witness at line number 16 of the prior page talks about it's the market attack, and in the text of the official English translation of the article, it says "as for the last market attack," I think there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's page 6 of the article in English and I can -- well, I can read it. It says -- before that it says: "Where approximately 70 people were killed the UN still maintains that it is not known who was responsible. However, we are almost certain that it was not the Serbs. There are certain rumours that an explosive device had been placed under a table ... as for the last market attack, the one that preceded the massive NATO raids against the Serbs," and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last -- the last is the last --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stand corrected again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sticking with this last market-place attack and your evidence that your statements were based on the reports of Military Observers, I want to show you 65 ter number 27315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we perhaps first ask when and under what circumstances he received the information which is at the basis of his -- unless that would disturb your line of questioning. If it does, then I'll withdraw but --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Always happy to take on board suggestions, Your Honour, so perhaps we could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, talking about this last market-place shelling, what form was the report that you received from the Military Observers? Was it written or was it oral?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Oral.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any written report from the UNMO Military Observers in respect of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I then, under those circumstances, again ask you: Where were you when you received that oral report about what you called the last shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm speaking of the last shelling, but, you know, for me there is only the one market-place shelling that I recall. There were several but this was the one I was involved in, and at that time I was in the PTT building where I had my office on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we are talking exclusively about one shelling and not one and then the last one, but it's all the same you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me, there is only one shelling that I speak of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are talking about the PTT building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have your indulgence for just a couple of moments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you got a copy, Mr. Segers, of the French-language interview that was published in Télé Moustique with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If not, I'd ask my friend to provide him with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, that should be with the ushers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we know what the solution would be, but where do we -- I think it's -- we have it still as a 65 ter number, the French version, in ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it D1466 MFI?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yep, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could we call that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can you go over to page 4 on the left-hand side. So that's -- go and look at the last page, Mr. Segers, of the one you have in front of you, the very last page, page 4, top right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in the original version, it's page 4, top right. And in the English version, this is on page 6. And maybe for Mr. Segers, if he wants to look at the screen, he could have a -- you could enlarge the far left-hand column in the original version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, here, in 1995, you're recorded as saying about halfway through the paragraph, and I'll say it in French so you could find your way. The sentence begins with [French spoken][No interpretation]. And then it continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're not getting translation of the French, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you found the spot I'm referring to, Mr. Segers?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English it's the fourth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Segers, when you talked about this situation and alleged that the UNMOs who investigated immediately after the catastrophe said that it was probable that it was launched -- that the shell in this case was launched by Muslims, what were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The formulation fired or detonated is not correct. It's about -- and I keep recurring to this, it is an explosive device alleged placed under one of the tables.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I'd like to leave you for a couple of seconds to have a look at this paragraph because the way I understand your evidence is that this paragraph relates to just one shelling. So have a look at the paragraph in the published interview for a second because I'd like to know if my understanding of your evidence is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I confirm that it is about a single shelling, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that single shelling that you're referring to in this paragraph, which you said in this paragraph happened in February 1994 and was the last -- it was the shelling that preceded the NATO raids against the Serbs. So two different things you said about it. So this single shelling, in your evidence, happened while you were stationed at the PTT building in that seven-month period between October 1992 and 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: The interview was done 20 years ago, and I can't really correctly even represent when I was in Sarajevo. What I do want to say is that, indeed, there was -- this concerns a shelling which was held as a following action and NATO intervened. For me, it concerns a -- a one-off shelling of the market -- of a market-place -- well, a shooting or an explosive device, let's be undecided about that. But I have a problem with dates, the dates, that's a problem, and I can't really recall. It's so long ago and to remember it then so exactly, I have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think in the interests of time, I'm going to move on --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have anything else before I leave this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to turn now to a final area. And since you've got your interview in front of you, just keep it open and go down to the bottom left-hand side where you mention that one of your colleagues -- it's about halfway down that paragraph. You mention an anecdote, and you say it was in May -- it -- last May where one of your colleagues saw Muslims firing a rocket against their television station. And that's at English page 6. Now I want to ask you about a question about that. So all you're doing here is reporting what your colleague in Zagreb told you about what had happened the year before; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're not only -- so you're completely unaware that this Chamber has heard evidence from another UNMO colleague, who is Mr. Brennskag, by the way, who actually -- who was on duty in his OP and actually saw the bomb - and it was a bomb, not a rocket - he saw the bomb being launched from VRS-held territory in Ilidza area and he followed it through the air until it hit the TV building. You don't know anything about that; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: When you ask me do I know anything about it because I was a witness to that, if that is your question, did I witness it, I will tell you no. But I saw numerous shootings and I didn't focus on this. I effectively gave you the story of what I heard from reliable sources at the time. However, you know probably as well as I do how much was going on in Sarajevo in that period. We wouldn't analyse every shot all the way in the air, which even just to do is very difficult, you know, try to follow with your eyes a projectile going through the air. It is not very obvious. So I have my doubt about whether this would be a very correct representation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have your doubt as to whether what your colleague told you is a correct representation? Or what I've just told you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I had complete faith in what my colleague told me or else I wouldn't have repeated it in the interview. What you're telling me now is something that I would doubt, and I would never, you know, negate what that person in question said. However, to follow a missile or a rocket or anything of artillery projectiles in the air is extremely difficult. But, you know, if he says that he did it, then it -- you know, that's what he says. However, I would stick by what I put on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you talk about a reliable source, do you think that the Bosnian Serb army's own documents might be a reliable source of information about what they did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just lost the thread. I just lost your question a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. When you talk about reliable sources, as you have been doing, do you think that the Bosnian Serb army's own documents might be a reliable source of information as to what they did?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would assume so. And I would assume that in the Bosnian Serb army, reports on what they did, the people, that that was correct. But what you mean, I think, is the reports of the Bosnian Serb army, rather than those of the observers on the side of the Bosnian Serb army. Because we had Military Observers on either side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did you know that on 30 June 1995, the commander of the Bosnian Serb army corps that surrounded Sarajevo confirmed that they fired on the TV building in retaliation for a military attack, and he was talking about exactly this case you mentioned? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall that today. I have no memory of that. I'm not going to say you -- no or yes, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just quickly pull up D147, please, and then we'll finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Something with -- in the English with the microphone, something's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that English words spoken are not received on channel 4. I do receive some -- I think now it has been fixed because I received the Dutch translation on channel 4. But now I think we have the English again, so could you please repeat what you'd like to -- I think you wanted D147?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct. D147, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar draws my attention to the fact that it's not a public document. Therefore, not to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh. Surprising. But can we go into private session to show it? Is it under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think -- you can -- it should not be shown to the public, which doesn't mean that no questions can be asked about it, but the document itself is protected. I don't remember for what reasons exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So the document is on the screen but it's not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Segers, I'd like you just to go down to the bottom part of the third paragraph in English where it says -- where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander says: "Our artillery forces are responding with precision -- are responding with precision to the Muslim artillery attacks. In one such response on 28 June, they hit the Bosnian radio and television centre, the centre of media lies against the just struggle of the Serbian people." So here's the corps commander confirming not only that they fired on the TV building where there was a civilian killed and 33 injured, they fired on it in retaliation for a military attack. Now, you said the different scenarios -- responding to the different scenarios I'd put to you, that you wouldn't negate what this person in question, your colleague in Zagreb, said. I want to know now, seeing this contemporaneous document, if you accept that the Bosnian Serb army launched a bomb at the TV building?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll object to the way that the question is phrased which implies that has been demonstrated that we're talking about the same incidents or if it was another bomb that was launched. The witness, as far as I know, has not identified a date. It is Ms. Edgerton that has introduced this particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then the parties are invited to present whatever evidence there is about an attack on the BH TV building. I mean, Ms. Edgerton, more or less you are asking this witness whether he would change his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is here to tell us what he knows and it is for up -- whether or not we consider that reliable and credible what he tells us depends on the total evaluation of the evidence, and you are more or less inviting the witness now to do the same on portions you have selected. I think the Chamber will, in the end, will be able to see whether the witness was talking about the same, whether there's any doubt about that, and what that would mean for the evaluation of the evidence, including the testimony of this witness and the interpretation of the document which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I use the time to tell that you D147, after some e-mail exchanges, is not any further a confidential exhibit and, therefore, could have been shown, but I wasn't aware of it at the time, and the formal status was still non-public, where it is now public.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes everything I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Segers, I will try to move as efficiently as possible. I apologise for you being here longer than anticipated. I would like to take up with the matter that was just raised by Ms. Edgerton as to the firing of a rocket or bomb at the TV building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to first call up 1D00796 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, as I did not foresee this and don't have a hard copy, but hopefully I will move slowly enough that we can follow the screen. This is a witness statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor by the individual whose name we see at the top. Sir, the first question I have for you is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why -- when -- when does this become leading? What's my friend doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know what the question will be. So to what extent it will be leading or not depends on what question. Perhaps Mr. Ivetic will ask whether the witness agrees that it's a white piece of paper. I don't know what his question will be. But certainly, Mr. Ivetic, you're alert now on any leading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the individual whose name appears at the top of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Well, I have vague recollection of a man called Hansen but whether this is this person, Thomas Hansen, remains really vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the statement in -- I think it's both languages. We have only the English on the screen, but in e-court there is a B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the fifth paragraph from the top, which I will read to you, and then I will have some questions about what is reflected here. And it starts: "I investigated" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is leading, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is leading?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He's going to read him the statement of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we do not know what --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- sorry, this man who is not a witness in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But we do not know yet what the question will be. I mean, you were very upset about just the name, but the question just was: Do you know that name? Of course, Mr. Ivetic could have asked that also without that document could -- are you familiar with the name of Thomas Hansen. But, Mr. Ivetic, please be aware that, of course, reading more may engage a risk of being leading, and therefore sometimes it is better to ask a question first and only then refer to what may be in the document that avoids often a risk of being leading. I leave it to you at this moment. We have not heard your question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think I'm following the procedure we've being using in this case since day one, so I'm a little confused by the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, in any event, I would like to read a portion of this statement to see if it refreshes your recollection of the particular incident that you are talking about in your statement when a colleague was declared persona non grata. If it does not, then I won't have any questions. But if it does, I will have follow-up questions. So it reads as follows: "I investigated among all the other shellings also an impact on the TV building on the 28 June 1995 that caused approximately 30 civilian casualties. I went first to the scene together with an UNMO. I was on the scene 20 minutes after the impact together with an UNMO. We had to wait approximately two hours for the arrival of the special investigation unit of the Bosnian police. "At that time we could not find any fragments or parts of the projectile that had hit the building. Normally we always get after an investigation the results of the Bosnian special unit. In this particular case, we never got any result. "In that period, there were a lot of homemade aeroplane bombs that landed in that area. It has to be about ten in the two weeks before the hit on the TV building. "On [sic] observation post could see that some of the [sic] bombs were fired from Ilidza on the BSA side. "I was informed by an UNMO who had seen the shelling on the TV building that this particular bomb that had [sic] impacted on the TV building was fired from the BiH side. Another UNMO who heard the bomb told me that the bomb only flew for a short period, so that fitted with the findings of the first UNMO that the bomb was fired from BiH-hold territory. I sent my report about this event to my superiors by secure means." Sir, does this incident sound like the one that you're talking about or is it another incident?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: This concerns another incident. I am not aware of an incident with so many casualties. In the period that I was in Sarajevo, there was a single shelling on the PTT building, direct to that building, effectively by a tank, and there was a single casualty. But otherwise, you know, this story seems not familiar to me. I mean, those facts are not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Now I'd like to try to clarify some other matters from your cross-examination. At temporary transcript page 12, lines 3 to 9 of the English transcript, you are recorded as saying as follows: "It was my job on behalf of the UB and in the Sector Sarajevo and the headquarters of the general at that time for the instructions they gave me which coincided with shooting incidents. Shooting between snipers and so on. With the -- to negotiate with the liaison officer from the other side to bring those to an end. And that happened both ways, both towards the Bosnians and toward the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo." And the question I have for you, sir, you are recorded as saying both towards the Bosnians and the Bosnian Muslims. Is that in fact what you meant to say or is there a word missing perhaps after Bosnians in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: My assignment was indeed for every incident by whatever party which would result in casualties, people hit, injured, or dead, that as soon as possible, we would liaise with the party in question to find a solution, a local cease-fire to begin with. And in individual cases of sniper fire, I do recall from the Serb side and I know there was anti-sniper fire also on the Bosnian side, but I don't recall, but this is after 20 years, that I had to intervene for shootings by snipers of the Bosnian -- Bosnian side. Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your quotation from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't catch the first part. The English feed wasn't coming through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your quotation from the transcript was correct when you said "UB," that was -- I noticed that as well, but the witness said "UN." But I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the next part I was going ask, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then moving on, at transcript page 20, lines 23 through 24 in the English language, you are recorded as saying that you saw outcoming fire from the centre of Sarajevo to the Kosevo Hospital. Is that, in fact, what you meant to say or is there a correction needed in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Might you repeat exactly where that is in the text again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not in the text, sir. It's in the transcript of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the transcript of today's hearing you are recorded as saying that you saw fire from the centre of Sarajevo to Kosevo Hospital and then the Serbs responded. And my question is in relation to that part that says that the fire came to Kosevo Hospital from the centre of Sarajevo. I'm not sure that's what you said, and I therefore give you the chance to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. First, there was outgoing fire from one of the pavilions surrounding the Kosevo Hospital and to that there was a response by Serb artillery. And this was not in the city. It was in the outer perimeter of the city from where there was firing. And we can't specifically say exactly it was this piece of artillery that fired. We can't say or prove that. We don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that adequately corrects that part of the transcript. Now, in relation to that incident at Kosevo Hospital, you indicated that the Serb liaison officer had called to complain and say, After five more minutes we will respond. Did the BiH side continue firing after that complaint was received, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I ... I cannot recall with certainty that there were further shootings. I know that the liaison officer at the time consented to a cease-fire, but it may have taken a while for that to filter through to the top, you know, through the Serb channels to go to the artillery shooters. There was a very short response from the Serb side. That I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you have, I think, explained to us today that you only know about this particular incident. Did you ever hear about other incidents where the BiH side placed weapons systems within the compound of Kosevo Hospital, perhaps from colleagues or from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. You have just told the witness that he has explained that this is the only incident that he knows about. Now you want to know whether he knows there are other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He testified this is the only incident he had first-hand knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not what you said. "And you have, I think, explained to us today that you only know about this" -- there's no word "first-hand."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I stand corrected. So let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So the question is -- you -- the question that you put, the answer thereto is the first sentence. He only knew about this one. Now you're forcing him to remember something else which he has told you he knows about one thing only.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I'm forcing the witness to do anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No -- "you have explained to us today that you only know about this particular incident. Did you ever hear about other incidents ..." Obviously if you heard about it, you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we have already confirmed that I misspoke and I meant to say: You know only about this incident first hand, which of course makes the question different, and I don't believe that I'm forcing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't say you misspoke. You just said: Yes, I accept that I didn't say so. You didn't say you misspoke. Again, you're coming up with something new.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but I'm not forcing the witness to say anything. I'm seeking to get an answer to a question if I may pose it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've made my point. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you told you have only first-hand knowledge of one incidence where there was outgoing fire from Kosevo Hospital and then an incoming response from the Serb side. My question is: Did you ever hear of other occasions where the Bosnian Muslim side placed weapons systems within the Kosevo Hospital compound irrespective of whether they fired them or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I can't answer that correctly because I don't recall. What I do know is about the case that I told you about that I was factually there, and of any other matters I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair, sir. That's fine. And you were asked by Ms. Edgerton about your arrival in Sarajevo and what was written in the Télé Moustique article as to the answer to the first question posed by the journalist. And this will be on page one of the French in the second and third column above your photo, and it is the middle of page 1 in the English, and we are talking about D1466 MFI. And Ms. Edgerton read the first part of that answer relating to women and children who became targets of an army, the Bosnian Serb army, and I would like to ask you about the last part of that answer, where you say: "I told myself at the time the weapons embargo on the Bosniaks needs to be lifted. Since then, after being on the ground in Bihac and in Croatia, I have changed my opinion." Could you explain for us how your opinion changed?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: When I came to Bosnia, I was confronted with so much misery. There were these heavy shootings, and as Madam Prosecutor said, this was the period in which there was no electricity, no heating, and then naturally at the time are you emotionally taken along with all that you see and especially what I saw on the Bosnian Muslim side. And at that moment it was my firm conviction that there wasn't a level playing field. It was unfair to take civilians as a victim over and against a military organisation. And in the period that I was there, in the course of that period I repeatedly saw that none of the parties were complying with the rules, the rules, quote/unquote, in as far as there were any in a conflict like that. And I had to conclude that, really, as they often say, that there is nobody innocent in a conflict. Everybody is more or less guilty, and this was definitely true. And even after negotiations of them -- liaisons on Muslim side, you know, much was promised and little was done, and you were given this story, if I can use that word, I thought there were three bad parties instead of just one, in my view, at the time, which doesn't mean that I didn't have great sympathy for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I believe my final question. You were asked about tank fire being a direct fire weapon. Can a tank also be used in indirect fire mode?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative. A tank is not necessarily -- do you know, really, it is not meant for indirect fire but it can be indirect fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's exactly my understanding as well. Sir, I thank you for being with us today and coming to testify. I have no further questions for you. And, again, I thank you heartily for your answers to my questions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I would have -- not many but at least one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reference was made to the published interview in which are you talking about the anecdote, the anecdote of something that happened in last May. Do you remember that? Or should we have it on our screen first?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: That might be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could we have the interview -- yes. And that's -- oh, it's there already. It's the fourth page. Page 4, lower part. Page 4 in the original, I meant, but ... page 4 in the French. And I don't know what page that would be in English. I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 6, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6 in English, yes. Yes. I take you there: "Another anecdote, last May or in" -- have you found it? Perhaps in French? [French spoken] [No interpretation]. That's ... left column as it appears now. No, it's further down. Further down. Further down. Yes, now the left column, "autre anecdote," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now another document was put to you in which a witness described an incident, and then Mr. Ivetic asked you whether that was the same incident as what you were referring to here in the interview by way of anecdote. You remember that? And then --

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were then asked whether it's -- whether that sounds like the one you're talking to in the interview. And I'll slowly read the answer: "This concerns another incident. I am not aware of an incident with so many casualties. In the period that I was in Sarajevo, there was a single shelling on the PTT building, direct to that, effectively by a tank, and there was a single casualty. But otherwise, you know, the story seems not familiar to me." Now when you were talking about the anecdote in the interview which was published, were you referring to that one incident, one single shelling of the PTT building? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Affirmative. I only ever knew of one incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, at the same time, you are giving this interview, 13 November 1995. "Last May" then would have been May 1995, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I understand your testimony well, you were not in Sarajevo at all at that time. So when you say, I was referring to one incident, the one that happened when I was in Sarajevo, in the interview, you strongly suggest that what you are talking about was happening at a time you were not in Sarajevo. So I'm a bit confused, and if you could assist me in better understanding how the anecdote you're talking about happened when you were in Sarajevo and, at the same time, it happened in May 1995, then that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I have to tell you honestly, I have returned so long ago, but what I want to say just very clearly is that in 1995, I was Military Observer at headquarters in Zagreb, and a number of facts that happened at the time in Sarajevo were followed by me by -- you know, from close-up because I was in the direct line of command and I would read all these reports, so I was even closer than actually being there. And now it has become very difficult, and it's not just the time, but in the meantime I have been victim of cancer and my memories have sort of partly left me, unfortunately. Was it a period in which I was actually there in Sarajevo in the PTT building, or was this in a period in which I was in Zagreb afterwards and was closely following matters. These are two things that are very difficult to distinguish after such a lapse of time. And so if I can simply explain how -- that also on my part there is a lack of clarity about what took place where, you know, I think this is -- this is the response I would give you, the explanation I would give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, in -- and, first of all, I'm sorry to hear that you suffered from cancer, but could you tell us how that affected your memory? What type of cancer was it? And if you'd rather speak about it in closed session, then we would move into private or closed session so that it -- your information remains within this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: No, no, I am one of the rare people who had breast cancer for men and so I had very heavy chemotherapy, and the oncologist simply confirmed to me that effectively this would affect one's memory temporarily, they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "temporarily," when were you treated?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: Two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would "temporary" mean only during the treatment or would it have an effect also after your treatment was concluded?

utterances.speaker: JAN SEGERS
utterances.text: I have five years of aftercare. The memory trouble is a trouble that would realise, well, temporarily, as the oncologists say, and it is passing, and I do see my memory improving. Because in the beginning, immediately after chemotherapy, and this took all of a year, there were serious lapses and blackouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that additional information. Any further questions, Ms. Edgerton? No further questions. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Segers, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- the Chamber feels sorry for Ms. Radovanovic, but we are facing the following problem. First of all, we need another break, which would leave us only 15 minutes, and then there are a few decisions which really have to be read out now and we couldn't wait for another weekend, et cetera. We always kept the non-urgent matters away if witnesses were waiting, but here, I'm afraid, that we have to proceed in reading those decisions. Now we have two possibilities, either -- first of all, Mrs. Radovanovic should be informed that the Chamber regrets highly that we are unable to continue to hear her evidence today and that we'd like to see her back on Monday morning. Second is what are we going to do now? We can take a break of 20 minutes and then read for 15 minutes decisions. We also could read them now and then adjourn a bit earlier. And to the extent Mr. Mladic would even consider whether to wait and hear all these decisions to be read, they are about the admission of associated exhibits tendered through Witness Akashi. There is one oral decision on the -- let me see whether there's any one in open -- there's one decision on admission of an expert report of Dusan Pavlovic. There is a decision on -- into evidence -- admission into evidence of P7809 and 7810, and there is a last decision which is about the admission of the expert report of Witness Dragic Gojkovic and four documents annexed. We leave it to Mr. Mladic either whether we read them now or after a break; and, second, whether he wants to be present when they're all read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm being told that we would prefer to have a break and then Mr. Mladic will remain after the break to listen to the decisions to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll take a break and we'll resume at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As announced, I'll deliver a few decisions. The first is the decision on the admission of associated exhibits tendered through Witness Yasushi Akashi. During the testimony of Witness Akashi, on the 23rd and 24th of November last year, the witness's Rule 92 ter statement comprising excerpts of his prior testimony in the Karadzic case was admitted as D1361. Of the 37 associated exhibits tendered with the statement, three had been admitted into evidence through other witnesses, and eight were then admitted into evidence during Akashi's testimony. In light of the Chamber's guidance to reduce the number of associated exhibits tendered, and given that there was insufficient time to address the remaining associated exhibits in court at the conclusion of Akashi's testimony on 17 December 2015, the Chamber gave the Defence one week to make submissions regarding the remaining 26 associated exhibits. On 24 December then, the Defence filed a motion to admit a reduced number of associated exhibits related to Akashi, pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Defence submits that these 13 documents are an essential and integral part of the witness's statement, without which the meaning of the statement would be incomplete or lost altogether, and therefore satisfy the test for admission of associated exhibits. The Prosecution has not objected to the Defence's motion. The Chamber will now decide on the admission of these 13 associated exhibits. The Chamber has reviewed the associated exhibits pursuant to Rule 89(C) and notes that they relate to the situation in Sarajevo and Srebrenica during 1994 and 1995. Twelve of the documents have a stamp, a signature or both, and thus bear sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity. The remaining document is an expert of an official parliamentary report on Srebrenica produced by the French National Assembly in 2001 and includes an interview with the witness. The Chamber is therefore satisfied that the documents tendered are relevant and have probative value. The Chambers recalls that documents can be admitted as associated exhibits if they are form an inseparable and indispensable of the witness's testimony. In order to satisfy this test, the tendering party must demonstrate that the witness's evidence would be incomprehensible or of a lesser probative value without the admission into evidence of the relevant associated exhibits. The Chamber has reviewed the associated exhibits in light of Akashi's statement. The witness was questioned about or otherwise discussed each of the associated exhibits in his statement to the extent that the Chamber finds that his statement would be incomprehensible, or of a lesser probative value, without the tendered documents. These documents therefore form an inseparable and indispensable part of Akashi's testimony. The Chamber hereby admits the following documents into evidence: Rule 65 ter numbers 1D02960, 1D04653, 1D04656, 1D04658, 1D04660, 1D04662, 03442, 03443, 03453, 03462, 08164, 10044, and 15738. The Chamber requests the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to these documents and to inform the parties and the Chamber of the numbers so assigned. As a final matter, the Chamber notes that e-court pages 3 and 4 of document bearing Rule 65 ter number 03443 are of a particularly poor quality. The Chamber would appreciate it if the parties could upload a more legible version of this document, if possible, and revert to the Chamber with regard to the same. And this concludes of Chamber's decision. I now move on to the Chamber's decision on the admission of Dragic Gojkovic's expert report and four documents annexed to that report. On 11 August 2015, Exhibit Number D1183 was reserved for Gojkovic's expert report pending an agreement between the parties on which excerpts of the report were to be tendered. On the 3rd of March of this year, the Defence notified the Chamber, by e-mail, that it had reached agreement with the Prosecution as to which excerpts of the report and which documents annexed to the report were to be tendered. The reduced version of Gojkovic's report was uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 1D05892b, and the four documents annexed to the report were uploaded under Rule 65 ter numbers 1D05772, 1D05773, 1D06182, and 1D06183. On the 9th and the 14th of March, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence, stating that it did not object to the admission into evidence of the report and the four annexed documents. The Chamber recalls the applicable law on the admission of expert evidence as set out in its decision of the 19th of October, 2012, concerning expert witness Richard Butler. The Chamber also recalls its oral decision of the 13th of May, 2015, granting Gojkovic the status of an expert on the destruction of religious buildings in Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995. The Chamber considers that the content of the expert report, which focuses, inter alia, on the destruction of religious sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995 and reviews the conclusions of Prosecution expert Andras Riedlmayer, falls within the scope of Gojkovic's expertise. Furthermore, the report relates to the charges set out in the municipalities component of the indictment and is therefore relevant to the case. Given the expertise of its author, the Chamber also considers the report to be probative for the purpose of its admission into evidence. The Chamber therefore finds that the requirements for admission into evidence have been met. The document bearing Rule 65 ter 1D06183 relates to the destruction of religious buildings in the municipalities included in the indictment. Concerning documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D05772 and 1D05773, certified photocopies of the complete lists of military personnel from the 1st Engineer Regiment and the 1st Pontoon Battalion of the 1st Krajina Corps, the Chamber notes that the related English translations have not been uploaded into e-court. However, the Chamber recalls that English translations of the relevant parts of these lists, namely, data concerning the Muslim and Croatian members of these units discussed by the witness in court on the 10th of August, are already admitted into evidence as Exhibit Numbers D1173, D1174, D1175, and D1176. With regard to document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D06182, the Chamber considers the document to be relevant for establishing the chain of custody of the two tendered military lists. The four documents bear indicia of authenticity such as stamps, signatures or information on the recipients and authors of the documents. The Chamber further finds that these documents are both relevant to the case and of probative value for the purpose of their admission into evidence. Therefore, the Chamber finds that the requirements for admission have been met. Accordingly, the Chamber instructs the Registry to reassign Exhibit Number D1183 to document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05892b and admits into -- admits it into evidence. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Trial Chamber admits into evidence documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D05772, 1D05773, 1D06182, and 1D06183, and instructs the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to these documents and notify the Chamber and parties when it has done so. This concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. Next decision to be delivered is a decision on the admission of Dusan Pavlovic's expert report and a related document. On the 14th of December, 2015, during Pavlovic's testimony, his expert report was marked for identification as D1373, pending the Chamber's consideration of the Prosecution's objections as set out in its notice dated 2nd of November, 2015. In that notice, the Prosecution challenged the expertise of the witness as well as the report's methodology and conclusions. In its 13th of November response to the Prosecution's notice, the Defence submitted that the report is reliable, methodologically sound, and admissible. Furthermore, on the 19th of April of this year, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution, by e-mail, that a corrected English translation of the report had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D33-0263. On the 25th of April, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence, by e-mail, that it does not object to the new translation. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the old translation of the report with the corrected one. On the 17th of December, 2015, the Defence tendered an additional document through Pavlovic which was marked for identification as D1399 and placed under seal. The Prosecution objected to its admission on the basis that the document had not been disclosed in a timely manner, lacked supporting materials, and should have formed part of the expert report. On the 1st of February of this year, the witness provided the parties with a more recent version of the document. On the 1st of March, this more recent version was admitted into evidence as Exhibit P7792 and placed under seal. The Chamber recalls the applicable law on the admission of expert evidence as set out in its decision on the 19th of October, 2012, concerning expert witness Richard Butler. With regard to the admissibility of the report, the Chamber recalls its oral decision of the 9th of December, 2015, granting Pavlovic's status as an expert in the tracing, exhumation, and identification of victims of war. Moreover, the Chamber considers that the content of the report which focuses on the losses incurred by the 28th Division of the ABiH during breakthrough out of Srebrenica in July 1995, as well as the fate of their remains, falls within the scope of Pavlovic's recognised expertise. Furthermore, as the report relates to the charges set out in the Srebrenica component of the indictment, the Chamber finds that it is relevant for the purposes of its admission into evidence. Lastly, as the report was authored by a recognised expert who testified about its methodology and conclusions and its sources are cited throughout, the Chamber finds the report to have probative value for the purposes of admission. For these reasons, the Chamber finds the report to be admissible and rejects the Prosecution's challenges concerning its methodology and conclusions. Turning to the admission of D1399, the Chamber notes that the document contains an overview of individuals who died during the ABiH breakthrough as discussed in the expert report and that the witness testified about the provenance of its content. The Chamber therefore finds D1399 to be relevant and of probative value for the purposes of admission. The Chamber considers the Prosecution's objection in relation to D1399 to be moot as the later version of this document was admitted as a Prosecution exhibit. Furthermore, the Chamber finds that although the admission of D1399 is to some extent superceded by the later version admitted as P7792, most of the witness's testimony related to the earlier version. Therefore, in the interests of a complete and clear record, the Chamber will exceptionally also admit D1399. Accordingly, the Chamber admits D1373 and D1399 into evidence, the latter being under seal. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Last decision to be read is a decision on the admission of P7809 and P7810, two UNMO Sarajevo patrol reports dated the 16th of March, 1995, which were marked for identification on the 1st of March, 2016, during the testimony of Per Oivind Oien. The Defence objected to the admission on the basis that their tendering was akin to the Prosecution reopening its case in-chief, as it was presenting evidence on a matter about which the witness did not testify during the Defence's examination-in-chief and "did not have additional facts to talk about." The Prosecution argued in response that the documents were admissible because: First, the Defence had broadened the scope of its examination-in-chief by discussing who was potentially motivated to fire at whom in Sarajevo; second, the witness had been called to testify about his time in Sarajevo; and, third, in light of the witness's testimony and former position, it was proper to confront him with information contained in certain documents that would have been available to him at the relevant time. The Chamber recalls the applicable law for admission of evidence contained in Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The Chamber further recalls its guidance of the 29th of October, 2012, in which it clarified that while it prefers that the witness through whom a document is tendered has personal knowledge about the document, probative value may also be established by the witness testifying about events described in the document. The guidance further stipulates that if the content of the document used during a witness's testimony is sufficiently linked to the content of that witness's testimony, the document may be appropriately tendered and admitted through that witness, whether or not the witness is familiar with the specific document. With regard to relevance, the Chamber finds that the documents are related, inter alia, to the alleged charges in the Sarajevo component of the indictment. With regard to the Defence's objections, the Chamber finds that the two UNMO Sarajevo patrol reports are within the scope of the witness's testimony since he was an UNMO deployed in Sarajevo as a Senior Military Observer from March until October 1995 and he received UNMO Sarajevo patrol reports during the period when he was deployed there. Therefore, the Chamber finds that the two documents have probative value for the purposes of their admission into evidence, are sufficiently linked to the content of the witness's testimony in accordance with the Chamber's 29th of October, 2012, guidance, and dismisses the Defence objections. The Chamber therefore finds that the requirements for admission pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules have been met. Pursuant to this same Rule, the Chamber admits P7809 and P7810 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume Monday, 2nd of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
